Half Moon Island, also known as Crescent Island, lies between Greenwich and Livingston Islands in the South Shetland Islands. About 2 km long, it has pebble beaches, low hills and outcrops of volcanic rock. Lichens grow on the rocks, while mosses and Antarctic flowering plants thrive among the stones.

Chinstrap penguins nest on the island and are recognisable by the narrow black band beneath their chins. Fur seals and Weddell seals also come ashore. The Argentine summer station Cámara stands in the western part of the island. Guides plan walking routes around the colonies and penguin paths; landings depend on sea conditions and the weather.

Hannah Point lies on the southern coast of Livingston Island. A narrow rocky promontory rises above the sea, with the beaches of Walker Bay nearby. Rocks, volcanic ash and coastal vegetation share this small area.

Gentoo and chinstrap penguins and southern giant petrels nest here. Elephant seals rest on the shore. During a walk, it is especially important to leave animals a clear route to the water; the accompanying guides choose the accessible route.

## Jarabacoa — a place for adventure!

The town lies in the heart of the country, in La Vega Province. Far from the sea, at an altitude of 529 metres, an entirely different kind of holiday awaits. Jarabacoa stands in the valley of the mountain river Jimenoa, whose rushing waters form a series of waterfalls. The largest, El Gran Salto de Jimenoa, has a drop of 20 metres. It is close to town and easy to visit on an excursion. Before descending to the waterfall, you can admire it from a convenient viewing platform above. A small pool has formed beneath the falls, where you can swim.

## A trip to the Jarabacoa nature reserve

Parque Nacional Jose Armando Bermudez is a remarkable protected natural area 35 kilometres west of Jarabacoa. Visitors come for picturesque views of high mountains and green valleys threaded with mountain rivers and streams, surrounded by olive groves, almond trees, palms, vines, blackwood and redwood trees, junipers and cedars.

## Closer to nature in Jarabacoa

The reserve is filled with the sounds of birdsong. Many bird species can be seen in the park, including nightingales, doves, Antillean crows, parrots, palm chats, woodpeckers and quails. You can explore the reserve on foot, on horseback or by bicycle. One of the most popular activities in the national park is climbing Pico Duarte, the highest peak in the Caribbean region.

Hidden Valley lies in western Belize, in the mountainous Mountain Pine Ridge area. Caribbean pines grow on the slopes, while dense tropical forest begins lower down. Walking trails wind between the hills, and streams form waterfalls and natural pools. People come here for forest walks, birdwatching and time spent surrounded by greenery.

You can spend several days in the private nature reserve: set out along a trail in the morning, return to the lodge in the afternoon and save another walk for the following day. The vegetation changes with altitude and the position of the slope, as open pine woodland gives way to humid thickets. Viewpoints overlook the Maya Mountains and forested valleys.

Hidden Valley fits naturally into a journey after Guatemala's archaeological sites and before Belize's Caribbean coast. The nearest town on the route is San Ignacio. Specific trails, access to waterfalls and guiding arrangements are agreed when booking: a walk within the reserve and additional excursions include different services.
